grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('vakapfeka')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'vakapfeka' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('Vanotamba')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'Vanotamba' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Colours & Describing Objects in Shona ('zvitema')
grammar_notes.content: This passage uses colour vocabulary such as 'zvitema'. Shona has three traditional core colour adjectives that change their prefix slightly to match the noun they describe: '-chena' (white/clean, e.g., 'ruvara ruchena' or 'shangu chena'), '-tema / nhema' (black/dark, e.g., 'mota nhema' or 'ruvara rutema'), and '-tsvuku' (red/bright brown, e.g., 'mota tsvuku' or 'ruvara rutsvuku'). For other colours like green ('girinhi'), blue ('bhuruu'), or orange ('orenji'), speakers typically say 'ruvara rwe-' ('the colour of...') followed by the colour name, as in 'ruvara rwegirinhi' (green).
grammar_notes.rule: Core Colours: -chena (white), -tema / nhema (black), -tsvuku (red) | Phrase pattern: ruvara rwe-[colour] (e.g., ruvara rwegirinhi)

cultural_notes.title: Shona Cultural & Everyday Context (Lesson 1)
cultural_notes.content: This expression ('Vakomana gumi vakapfeka zvikadabura zvitema uyezve vakapfeka matishetsi eyero ane makora matema.Mukomana mumwe chete akapfeka ngowani tema.Vakomana gumi vose ava vakapfeka shangu dzakavhurika dzisina tambo.Vanotamba nhabvu.' — "People komana gumi they (past) pfeka things kadabura things tema uyezve they (past) pfeka plural tishetsi eyero ane plural kora plural tema.mukomana in / singular mwe chete he/she (past) pfeka ngowani tema.vakomana gumi.") reflects how Shona speakers connect daily family life, work, and community relationships across urban towns and rural homesteads ('kumusha') in Zimbabwe.

active_exercises.prompt: Complete this sentence about tree leaves: 'Mashizha emuti uyu ane ruvara ______.' (The leaves of this tree have a green colour.)
active_exercises.explanation: 'Ruvara rwegirinhi' expresses 'green colour' when describing fresh leaves ('mashizha').

active_exercises.prompt: Translate this new sentence into English: 'Mukoma wangu akatenga mota chena nezuro.'
options: My older brother bought a white car yesterday.
My sister is wearing a red dress today.
Which bus goes to the city centre?
The black truck is parked beside the road.
active_exercises.correct_answer: My older brother bought a white car yesterday.
active_exercises.explanation: 'Mukoma wangu' = 'My older brother', 'akatenga' = 'bought', 'mota chena' = 'a white car', 'nezuro' = 'yesterday'.

active_exercises.prompt: Your friend just passed her driving test! What do you say to congratulate her in Shona?
active_exercises.explanation: 'Makorokoto!' means 'Congratulations!' and 'nekubudirira kwako' means 'on your success'.
